title: Four fingers, one filter
teaches: Paraphonic and unison voices, voice stealing, and chords from one key

parts.title: A chord that breathes as one

blocks.text: **The mystery.** This synth has played one note at a time for seventeen lessons. Below, it plays chords. Listen to the brightness, which swells with each chord. Every note of each chord opens and closes at the same moment, as if one hand were sweeping one filter for all of them. On a piano, or in a band of three players, each note would have its own shape. Why do these move together?

blocks.caption: Four chords, first on a one-note synth, then on a paraphonic one

blocks.text: Because there *is* only one filter. The synth has grown four oscillators, one per finger, but they all feed into the same filter and envelope. That arrangement is called **paraphonic**: several pitches, one sound-shaping path. With one note at a time, as before, it is **monophonic**.

The voice mode switch below has three settings. **Mono** plays one note: only one note of each chord in the loop, or the last key you pressed. **Para** plays up to four, sharing the filter and envelope. Switch it, and play some chords on the keys: hold three keys down together.

blocks.caption: A slow, swelling patch on four chords. Switch it to paraphonic.

blocks.text: A paraphonic synth has a quirk you will hear as soon as you play it like a piano. The envelope belongs to all the notes at once, so pressing a new key starts it again for every note already sounding: the whole chord re-swells. And on a four-note synth, a fifth key has to take the place of one already held. Choosing which note gives way is called **voice stealing**; this synth, like most, drops the oldest.

A **polyphonic** synth gives each note a whole voice, with its own oscillators, filter and envelopes. A chord on a polyphonic synth is several complete synths playing at once, each note shaped separately, like a piano.[^poly] That takes a filter and envelopes for every note, which is why polyphony was expensive for so long, and why small synths today are often paraphonic: extra oscillators are cheap, extra filters are not.

blocks.caption: A Prophet-5 that Richard Wright of Pink Floyd took on tour in 1980, with his settings for each song written on the panel.

blocks.text: Paraphony has its own uses. A pad on a paraphonic synth sweeps as one block, which can sound bigger and more deliberate than a polyphonic one. Played one note at a time, it is a mono synth, with glide and legato from lesson 17 still working. What it cannot do is let a held chord ring on while a new note plucks over it: the new note re-plucks the lot.

The third setting, **Unison**, uses the four oscillators the other way: all on the same note, each tuned a few cents apart. It is lesson 5's two detuned oscillators taken further. The result is one very thick note, the sound of many big synth leads and basses. **Spread** sets how far apart they are tuned.

blocks.caption: A plain lead, the sound that plays a tune. Stack it in unison and spread the tuning.
blocks.task: Unison, with a spread of 30 cents or more

blocks.text: A little spread thickens the sound; a lot of spread starts to sound out of tune, then like a crowd. Unison is a mono mode: every oscillator is busy on the one note, so it cannot play chords, and the chord switch below does nothing in it.

The last trick turns one key into a chord. The **Chord** switch adds fixed intervals above whatever you play: an octave, a fifth, or the extra notes of a minor, major or suspended chord.[^chord-colours] Every key then plays the same chord shape, moved up or down. It is a mono line played in chords, through the one filter.

blocks.caption: A short pluck on the offbeat. Step through the chord shapes.

blocks.text: Early-1980s synths had the same idea as **chord memory**, storing whatever chord you held and giving it back on every key. Played as a short pluck, this is the **stab** of house and techno: one chord shape moved up and down, never changing its internal intervals. Because every note carries the same shape, a one-finger bass line becomes a chord line without anyone needing to know harmony.[^stab]
Now make it. The patch below is a dark pluck on the offbeat, one note at a time. Make it a minor-chord stab, and open the filter enough for the chord to cut through.

blocks.caption: A dark single-note pluck. Make it a minor stab.

blocks.text: Play it on the keys and every key gives the same chord shape, which is why it suits a quick riff. On an unfamiliar synth, look for a switch or menu that says Mono, Para, Poly, Unison or Legato, and a Chord or Hold button. Together they decide what happens when more than one key goes down, and they are often the reason a patch sounds thin, or refuses to play the chord you just pressed.

blocks.caption: Five questions on voices
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

choices: Several pitches through one shared filter and envelope
Each note with its own filter
items.why: Paraphonic synths share the sound-shaping path between their notes.

items.ask: On a paraphonic synth, you hold a chord and press one more key. What happens to the held notes?
choices: Their envelope starts again with the new note
items.why: The envelope belongs to every note, so a new key restarts it for all.

items.ask: What does unison do with the oscillators?
choices: Puts them all on one note, slightly detuned
Turns them off one by one
items.why: Unison stacks every oscillator on the same pitch, spread apart in tuning.

items.ask: A four-note paraphonic synth: you press a fifth key. What is that called?
items.why: One of the held notes has to give up its oscillator.

items.ask: With the chord switch on a minor chord, what does every key play?
choices: A minor chord built on that key
items.why: Chord memory adds the same shape above whatever key is played.

summary: **Monophonic plays one note**; paraphonic plays several pitches through one filter and envelope.
**On a paraphonic synth the envelope belongs to the whole chord**: a new key re-swells every note.
**Polyphonic gives each note a whole voice**, with its own filter and envelopes.
**Voice stealing**: with every voice busy, a new key takes the oldest note's place.
**Unison stacks every oscillator on one note**, detuned by the spread, for a thick mono sound.
**Chord memory makes one key play a fixed chord shape**: the house and techno stab.
**On a strange synth, find the voice mode first** when it won't play the chord you pressed.

poly.title: Five voices
poly.text: Polyphonic synths existed earlier in the 1970s, but the one that set the pattern was the Sequential Circuits Prophet-5 of 1978: five complete voices, each with two oscillators, a filter and two envelopes, plus a microprocessor that stored whole patches and assigned voices to keys. Before polyphonic synths, a player who wanted chords with independent shapes had to record a mono synth one note at a time onto separate tape tracks.

stab.title: Chord memory
stab.text: Several synths of the early 1980s, the Korg Polysix and Roland Juno-60 among them, had a button that stored whatever chord was held and played it from any single key afterwards. House and techno producers later in the decade used it to turn a one-finger riff into a riff of chords, and the stab became one of the commonest sounds in dance music.

chord-colours.title: Major, minor and suspended
chord-colours.text: A three-note chord (a triad) is built from the root note you press, a fifth above it (seven semitones), and a middle note that sets its colour. A major chord puts that middle note four semitones above the root and sounds bright; a minor chord puts it at three semitones and sounds darker; a suspended fourth puts it at five semitones, sounding open and unsettled.
